name: Anglefrauding

lead: Anglefrauding is looksmaxxing slang for using camera positioning to look better in photos. Changing the height of the camera, the tilt of the head, the lens distance and the lighting alters how facial features appear in a picture.
In communities, people post face photos for ratings and often mention whether the picture is angle-frauded. Threads discuss it alongside makeup as a way to present the face well [1].

paras: People experiment with camera height and head tilt, distance from the lens, and lighting until a flattering image results, and often pair this with makeup or grooming [1].

The main downside discussed is a gap between photos and real-life appearance, which can affect how ratings or first meetings in person are received. Community threads debate whether the practice is acceptable [2].

angle.text: People use camera positioning to make photos of their face look better, often alongside makeup. The change affects the image, not the face itself.

lead: Anglefrauding (also angle fraud or angle frauding) is a term from looksmaxxing forums for choosing camera position, head pose, distance and lighting so that a photo presents the face more favourably than a typical or neutral view would. It is widely used in rating threads, where users note that a photo is only "slightly" angle-frauded or call out photos that appear heavily so [1].

The appearance goal is a better-looking image. The same face can show a stronger-looking jaw, larger-looking eyes, a smaller-looking nose or smoother skin depending on camera height, lens distance, head tilt and light. Community threads link the practice to makeup as another way of managing presentation [2], and the practice is a low-cost way to put the best available version of one's face in front of raters, dating-app viewers or employers.

Photography and face-perception research supports the underlying premise that photographs of one face vary in perceived attractiveness. Studies have found that camera distance changes ratings of attractiveness, trustworthiness and competence [3], that a close selfie enlarges the apparent nose [4], that head tilt shifts perceived attractiveness and dominance [5], and that unfamiliar viewers rate different photos of the same person as very different in attractiveness [6]. The forum term itself has not been studied.

paras: Anglefrauding refers to deliberately choosing viewpoints and poses that flatter the face. Participants in rating threads often qualify their photos with notes such as "angle frauding slightly" so reviewers can account for it [1]. The word frauder is used for someone who is skilled at it, sometimes as a joke about who is the most capable at it [7].

The levers are the ordinary ones of portrait photography. Camera height changes how the jaw, neck and eye area read; chin and head tilt change apparent facial proportions; distance and lens focal length change how large near features look relative to far ones; and light direction changes how bone structure, skin and shadows appear. Photography references explain that perspective depends mainly on subject-to-camera distance, that wide-angle portraits taken close tend to enlarge the nose, and that longer lenses flatten features, with 85 to 135 mm (35 mm equivalent) commonly cited for portraits [8].

The term belongs to the vocabulary of the looksmaxxing and PSL forums. Wikipedia describes looksmaxxing as a neologism from incel-era message boards in the 2010s, centred on rating forums, where a culture of rating faces made photo conventions such as front and side angles, neutral expression and lighting matter, and where rating threads remain a major activity [9]. That rating culture is the setting in which "angle fraud" arose: since people were scored from photographs, how the photograph was taken affected the score.

The word carries a mild accusation. A thread asks outright whether the practice is bad [10], while others discuss it alongside makeup as a lever on appearance in photos [2] or relate it to craniofacial structure and the limits of what one can change through growth [11]. Opinions differ on whether it is a legitimate way of presenting oneself or a misrepresentation, particularly when photos are used on dating profiles.

sections.h: Research on camera angle, distance and pose
paras: Camera distance. In a 2012 PLOS ONE study, Ronnie Bryan, Pietro Perona and Ralph Adolphs of Caltech photographed the same faces at the same moment from 45 cm and 135 cm using a half-silvered mirror. Faces from the farther position were rated higher in attractiveness, trustworthiness and competence in several experiments, with small effect sizes (Cohen's d from about 0.14 to 0.31) [3]. Viewers did not notice the manipulation [3].

Selfie distortion. A 2018 JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery modelling study by Brittany Ward, Max Ward, Ohad Fried and Boris Paskhover calculated that at 12 inches the nose appeared about 30 percent larger in men and 29 percent in women than in an orthographic view, with negligible distortion at 5 feet; the authors noted that close photos misrepresent the nose's true three-dimensional proportions [4]. Coverage of the study quoted Paskhover likening a close selfie to a portable funhouse mirror [12].

Head tilt. A 2020 Evolutionary Psychology study by Peter Marshall, Amy Bartolacci and Darren Burke, using software-generated faces, found that tilting female faces downward increased ratings of attractiveness and femininity, that masculinity rose as male faces tilted upward, and that male attractiveness peaked at a slight downward angle [5]. The authors noted that raters could not tell whether differences reflected head tilt or the target's height [5].

Photo-to-photo variability. Rob Jenkins of the University of Glasgow and colleagues reported in Cognition in 2011 that photos of one person differed substantially in perceived identity and in rated attractiveness; students rated some photos of the same unfamiliar person as good-looking and others as unappealing [6].

The term is used both as a self-description and as an accusation when someone's photos differ from their in-person look. Users post photos for ratings with a note about how angle-frauded they are, and responders sometimes account for it when scoring [1]. In the threads' framing, the practice sits beside makeup, lighting and editing as part of presenting a face [2], and beside a separate line of discussion about what the camera cannot change, such as craniofacial structure [11].

Media coverage of looksmaxxing since 2023, including features in The New York Times, The Guardian, BBC, GQ and NPR, has focused on surgery, drugs and rating culture rather than photography technique [9].

The main downside discussed in forums is a gap between photos and real-life appearance, which can affect how ratings or first meetings are received. Researchers who study selfies have raised a related concern: Paskhover argues that people who treat selfies as accurate portraits may develop distorted self-images [12], and a survey summarised on Wikipedia found 42 percent of surveyed facial plastic surgeons had seen patients seeking procedures to look better in photos [13].
No studies found on anglefrauding as a practice. Related laboratory research on camera distance, selfie distortion, head tilt and photo variability is described above [3][4][6][5].

lore.intro: The practice is discussed in several looksmax.org threads, from jokes about skilled practitioners to debates over whether it is acceptable [10][1][7].

Jenkins and colleagues publish a study on variability in photos of the same face, including attractiveness ratings [6].
Bryan, Perona and Adolphs report camera distance effects on rated attractiveness [3].

Marshall, Bartolacci and Burke publish a study on head tilt, attractiveness and dominance [5].
Press coverage brings looksmaxxing to mainstream audiences [9].
